ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Amendment of Indian Forest Act, 1927 
  *181. SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI:                                                                                                  
     DR. T SUBBARAMI REDDY: † 
Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government are considering to amend the Indian Forest 
Act, 1927; 
(b) if so, whether Government have also decided to pass the 
Scheduled Tribes (Recognition of Forest Rights) Bill; 
(c) whether the Forest Conservation Act, 1980 which expanded IFA's 
scope by centralizing State powers over forests made the prior approval 
of the Central Government necessary for dereservation of reserved forests 
for use of forest land for non-forest purposes; and 
(d) by what time the Bill is likely to be introduced and passed? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) to (d) A 
Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
†The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Dr. T. Subbarami 
Reddy. 

                               RAJYA SABHA             [5 August, 2005] 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir. The Government of India is considering amendment to 
Indian Forest Act, 1927 to meet the objectives of National Forest Policy 
in a holistic manner for the maintenance of environmental stability through 
preservation and restoration of ecological balance, meeting requirement 
of fuel wood, fodder, minor forest produce and small timber to rural and 
tribal population with their involvement. 
(b) Ministry of Tribal Affairs in the Union Government is formulating 
"The Schedule Tribes (Recognition of Forest Rights) Bill, 2005. 
(c) Yes, Sir. 
(d) The proposed Bills-The Schedule Tribes (Recognition of Forest 
Rights) Bill, 2005 and Amendment to Indian Forest Act, 1927 are still at 
a draft stage and to be finalized as per the established procedure. No time-
frame can be indicated at this stage regarding introduction of the Bills. 
DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: Sir, the hon. Minister has not given a 
proper and a clear reply. When we asked as to whether the Government 
was considering amending the Indian Forest Act, 1927 he has stated, 
"The Government of India is considering amendment to Indian Forest 
Act, 1927, to meet the objectives of National Forest Policy in a holistic 
manner for the maintenance of environmental stability through 
preservation and restoration of ecological balance." Here, I would like to 
know what improvements the Government is contemplating in this new 
legislation. And, what will be the difference between the 1927 Act and 
the proposed legislation? 
SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA: Sir, the draft legislation is under 
consideration. We are going to amend the Indian Forest Act which would 
ensure environmental stability and preservation of natural heritage, and 
safeguard bio-diversity. The proposed amendments include (i) Action 
Plan by Forest Police and Revenue Officers to prevent encroachments; 
(ii) involvement of Joint Forest Management in the matter of 
conservation and management of forests; (iii) provision for relaxation and 
transit of various produce; (iv) rehabilitation of 15 cultivation areas for 
plantation; and (v) diverting and shifting of cultivation into settled 
cultivation in the affected areas.

DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: Sir, my second supplementary is this. 
The Forest Conservation Act, 1980, expanded the IFA's scope by 
centralising the State powers over the forests and made the prior appro\ 
H\ of the Central Government necessary. Sir, everybody is very much 
interested in the preservation of forests in the country. At the same 
time, in the forest areas, if there is a proposal to construct hospitals or 
irrigation dams or to do some mining, or putting up new factories 
which will create employment, there is this hard feeling amongst 
people that wherever any permission is required from the Ministry of 
Environment and Forests to support these national projects, they always

Minister what mechanism the Ministry has got in this regard and how 
he isf going to ensure that they do not come in the way of increased 
industrial production in the country. 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI A. 
RAJA): Basically, the Forest Conservation Act itself is not a 
prohibitory Act. It is only a regulatory Act. So, it is not that the 
developmental activities are scuttled.... 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Are you talking about the Forest Conservation Act, 
1980? 
SHRI A. RAJA: Yes, Sir. The Forest Conservation Act of 1980 is a 
regulatory Act under which developmental activities are permitted. As 
a matter of fact, so far, 12,241 projects were permitted under this Act. 
In fact, 10.03 lakh hectares of forest lands have been given for 
developmental activities. The main object of the Act is that 
conservation must be protected, while, at the same time, permitting 
developmental activities. In other words, developmental activities and 
conservation should go hand-in-hand. In other words, this approach of 
synchronisation means that developmental activities are not scuttled 
because of protection of the forests. That has been contemplated in the 
Forest Conservation Act. Of course, in the guidelines, schools, school 
buildings, dispensaries and hospitals, electrical and communication 
lines, drinking water supply, minor irrigation canals, non- conventional 
sources of energy, power sub-stations, are all permitted under the Forest 
Conservation Act. Some liberal approach has been there, so far as the 
State Governments are concerned.

Anthrax disease 
 *182. SHRI N.K. PREMACHANDRAN: Will the Minister of 
HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether any State in the country is under Anthrax threat and if so, the 
details of cases of Anthrax disease reported so far, State-wise; 
(b) the precautions proposed to be taken by Government to check the 
disease; and 
(c) whether any pakcage of assistance has been made available to the 
State Governments under the Centrally sponsored schemes to control the 
disease? 
 THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of 
the House. 
Statement 
Natural anthrax is endemic in some parts of the country. It had been 
reported from Orissa (2000-2005) Karnataka (2001 & 2004), Andhra 
Pradesh (2000, 2001, 2004 & 2005), Tamil Nadu (2005), West Bengal 
(2001, 2003, 2004 & 2005). The details of cases reported so far since 
2000 are annexed as Statement-I. (See below) 
Anthrax is primarily a disease of animals. Humans can become infected 
with Anthrax while handling products from infected animals (Cutaneous 
Anthrax) or breathing infected spores (Inhalation Anthrax) and by eating 
of undercooked meat from infected animals (Gastrointestinal Anthrax). 
8 

[5 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
The important strategies are surveillance among animals, vaccination, 
early treatment of animals, disinfection, safe disposal of carcases and 
Information, Education and Communication activities. 
Whenever an outbreak is reported, the National Institute of 
Communicable Diseases (NICD) conducts epidemiological investigations 
and advise the State on the public measures and each time the disease has 
been contained effectively. NICD also provides necessary guidelines and 
laboratory support. 
The State health authorities institute the public health measures which 
includes daily monitoring and reporting of cases by district health 
authorities, early diagnosis and treatment, ensuring adequate stock of 
medicines, intensifying IEC activities. 
Under the Integrated Disease Surveillance Project (IDSP) launched by 
Government of India in November, 2004, to establish a decentralized 
state based system of surveillance for communicable and non-
communicable diseases, each state has been given the option to identify 
up to five endemic conditions for surveillance in addition, to a list of core 
conditions under surveillance for all States. Thus, States where Anthrax is 
a problem can include the disease as one of the five conditions.

 SHRI N.K. PREMACHANDRAN: Sir, the Anthrax disease has mainly 
occurred in pockets of Southern States of Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, 
Karnataka, Union Territory of Pondicherry and some parts of West 
Bengal and Orissa. Sir, lndia is considered as an endemic region for the 
animal Anthrax because of a large unprotected and uncontrolled 
livestock population. Also, most of the human Anthrax cases occur to 
agricultural labourers who have the history of handling animal meat or 
skin of infected animal. My point is, in order to control and contain this 
Anthrax disease, public awareness is needed. So, I would like to know 
from the hon. Minister what steps are being taken by the Government to 
create awareness regarding this communicable disease of Anthrax. 
 DR. ANBUMANI RAMDOSS: Sir, as the hon. Member has rightly 
said, the animal Anthrax has been endemic in about five States, namely, 
West Bengal, Orissa, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka and a 
little bit in Pondicherry. Every year, we have a little outbreak, mostly in 
Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and West Bengal, mostly in the 
tribal areas where there is not much awareness. 
 Sir, there are three types of Anthrax. One is the cutaneous Anthrax where 
it comes from the skin; another is inhalationAnthrax, which if one is 
exposed to spores of Anthrax, that is a very serious Anthrax; and the third 
is the gastro-intestinat Anthrax, when you take the meat of an animal 
which has Anthrax. The awareness has bean created, is being created, 
both by the Central and State Governments about not to eat infected food 
and to bury the dead animals.or to burn them and also to vaccinate the 
high-risk group, that is, persons who are handling this meat or cattle, and 
also sometimes during wool manufacturing facilities where inhalation 
Anthrax could be there. All those persons can be vaccinated. In fact, there is 
an international vaccine also available. And, mostly, not only to the people 
but to the health-care providers also. A lot of exercise is being done to see 
how to identify. Surveys have been done. A lot of survey network has been 
formed to these endemic area, in fact, with the Govemment of India's 
supplement, through the National institute of Communicable Diseases, 
whenever there is an outbreak, immediately we go there and advise the 
State Government and we have a coordination with them. Not only the 
Health Ministry, but even the Animal Husbandry Ministry also is taking an 
active interest; in fact, last year, through Centrally-sponsored programmes, 
37.18 lakh cattle have been vaccinated to prevent this. Definitely, Sir, we 
are concerned about this Anthrax in the endemic areas and we want to 
totally eradicate and eliminate this.

not have a viable Indian vaccine for humans; we have an international

Impact of Patent Laws on pharma sector 
  
 *185. SHRI KB. KRISHNA MURTHY: † 
            SHRI HARISH RAWAT 
 Will the Minister of CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have assessed the impact of recent Patent Laws on 
the restructuring of pharma sector in the country; 
(b) if not, the reasons therefor; 
(c) if so, whether such restructuring would cause the closure of some units; 
(d) if so, what will be the extent of unemployment due to closure of units; 
and 
(e) what steps are being taken to absorb the skilled manpower of the closed 
units? 
 THE MINISTER OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI RAM 
VILAS PASWAN): (a) to (e) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
 (a) to (e) India is a signatory to the agreement establishing the World Trade 
Organisation. The WTO Agreement, inter-alia, contains an 
†The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri KB. Krishna Murthy 
27 

RAJYA SABHA                     [5 August, 2005] 
agreement on IPR, namely, the Agreement on Trade Related Aspects of IPR 
(TRIPS). The TRIPS Agreement requires member countries to align their 
legislations on intellectual property in conformity with their obligations under the 
TRIPS Agreement. In respect of Patents, the TRIPS Agreement prescribed 
introduction of product patents from 1. 1.2005, for pharmaceutical, food and 
agrochemical inventions. Accordingly, product patent protection has been 
provided by amending Indian Patents Act. 1970. 
 While considering the amendments to the Indian Patents Act, 1970 elaborate 
consultations were carried out with all the concerned Departments of the 
Government of India and also with the various concerned organisations and 
industry associations including the prominent associations of the pharmaceutical 
industry. The concerns and apprehensions projected by the pharmaceutical 
industry, including the impact on the pharmaceutical sector as a whole, have been 
by and large been given consideration and adequate safeguards to ensure the 
continued availability of medicines at reasonable prices have been incorporated in 
the law while finalising the amendments. 
 It is estimated that over 95 per cent of the drugs being produced in India are 
off-patent and would not be affected by the introduction of product patent. 
Similarly the medicines included in the National List of Essential Medicines, 
2003 are also off-patent and would not be affected by the product patent regime. 
The small number of drugs (less than 5 per cent) which are likely to be covered 
under product patent would continue to be produced in the country without any 
interruption. This has been ensued under the latest amendment in the Indian 
Patents Act, 1970. A reasonable royalty on the production of such drugs would 
become payable to the patent-holder company. 
 Since production of the existing drugs being produced in lndia would not be 
affected by the introduction of product patent regime there is no likelihood of 
closure of some of the units due to this reason. As such there is no question of 
unemployment in the pharma industry taking place in India due to introduction of 
product patent regime.

(c) The Government has launched the Na tional Rural Health Mission (NRHM) 
on 12th April, 2005. It seeks to provide effective health care to rural population 
particularly poor and vulnerable sections through out the country with special focus 
on 18 States which includes 8 Empowered Action Group (EAG) States, 8 North-East

from 2005-12. The total outlay for the National Rural Health Mission for the year 
2005-06 is Rs. 6731.15 crore. The recommendations of the Planning Commission 
in MTA are also part of the future action programme of the Ministry of Health and 
Family Welfare.

Two child norm 
 †*188. SHRI RAJ MOHINDER SINGH MAJITHA: 
SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that it is necessary to follow two child norm in the 
family to control the population of the country; 
(b) if so, the reaction of Government in this regard; 
(c) whether it is a fact that several St ate Governments in the country have

(d) if so, the names of the States and the steps taken by them in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) and (b) The Family Welfare Programme in 
India is voluntary in nature, which enables a couple to adopt the family 
planning methods, best suited to th em, according to their choice, without any 
compulsion. They are free to decide the size of their family. The policy of the 
Government is to promote small family norm without prescribing any number 
of children. 
(c) and (d) The Government has advised States/UTs to formulate their State 
Population Policy with State specific st rategies maintaining the general spirit 
of voluntary and non-coercive approach as envisaged in National Population 
Policy, 2000. 
However, certain States like Andhra Pradesh, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, 
Madhya Pradesh, Maharastra, Rajasthan, Orissa and Delhi have adopted 
policies based on two child norm. The measures adopted by the States include 
provisions for disqualifying persons having more

*193. SHRI R.K. ANAND: Will the Minister of  HEALTH AND FAMILY

(a) whether it is a fact that his Ministry had announced setting up a separate

prevalence of communicable, non-communicable and pollution-related

(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that the Indian Council of Medical Research had an

THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) to (d) The Ministry of Health & Family Welfare 
is considering setting up National Disease Surveillance Authority to work as a 
multi-disciplinary organization undertaking surveillance, outbreak 
investigation and response and related operational research. The Authority will 
not only monitor the incidence of illnesses but will also prepare response teams

The Ministry of Health and Family  Welfare is implementing a World 
Bank assisted Integrated Disease Surveillance Project (IDSP) (2004-09) in a 
phased manner all over the country since November, 2004. This project has 
an outlay of Rs. 408.36 crores. The project involves the designing and 
operationalising of a dedicated Information Technology network throughout 
the country for disease surveillance. This  network will assist in decentralized 
collection of illness statistics and rapid transmission of epidemiological data. 
Specialised software are proposed to monitor the trigger levels and alerts 
regarding individual illnesses. The project is receiving assistance from several 
partners and stakeholders including  National Technical Institutions like 
ICMR, NICD and CBHI etc. ICMR is only involved in the process of 
surveillance of risk factors of non- communicable diseases and providing 
technical, assistance to the project. 
Though disease surveillance and medi cal research are closely related 
activities, the inputs and expertise required for both are very different. 
Therefore, a research-based organization may not necessarily be best suited 
for carrying out disease surveillance.

THE MINISTER OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI RAM 
VILAS PASWAN): (a) to (c) Presently 74  bulk drugs specified in the First 
Schedule of the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 1995 (DPCO, 95) and the 
formulations based thereon are under price control and their prices are 
fixed/revised by the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) in 
accordance with the provisions of th e DPCO, 95. These drugs have been 
identified for inclusion under price control in the DPCO, 95 on the basis of 
criteria mentioned in the 'Modifications in Drug Policy, 1986', announced in 
September, 1994. These criteria take into account the extent of usage and the 
market competition in various drugs. While calculating the prices of Scheduled 
formulations manufactured indigenously, Maximum Allowable Post 
Manufacturing Expenses (MAPE) is allowed @ 100% on ex-factory cost and in 
the case of imported Scheduled formulations MAPE is allowed upto 50% of the 
landed cost. 
Prices of non-Scheduled formulations are fixed by the manufacturers 
themselves keeping in view the various factors like cost of production, 
marketing/selling expenses, R&D expe nses, trade commission, market 
competition, product innovation, product quality etc. Due to these factors there is 
a wide variation between the production cost and selling price of these 
medicines. The Government takes corrective measures where the public interest 
is found to be adversely affected. 
In accordance with Notification No. 2/2005-Central Excise (NT.) dated the 
7th January, 2005 read with Notification No. 4/2005-Central Excise (NT.) 
dated the 23rd February, 2005 of Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance, 
excise duty is being levied, wherever chargeable, on the basis of retail price of 
medicines after granting an abatement of 40% of retail price. Retail price 
based levy of excise duty is to facilitate assessment and provides uniformity. 
The change in the mode of assessment of excise duty on drugs is not expected to 
have a major impact on the retail prices of drugs and medicines. 
As regards VAT, it may be mentioned after implementaton of VAT w.e.f. 
01.04.2005 the retail prices of most of the medicines are expected to come 
down because the rate of VAT is 4% only throughout the country where VAT 
is implemented as compared to sales tax rate which was earlier varying from 
8% to 13% in different States. However, the retail prices of medicines may 
not come down due to VAT in those States 
43 

RAJYA SABHA [5 August, 2005] 
where VAT has not been implemented and the existing rate of sales tax is being followed. 
Further in some, States, certain drugs were exempted from sales tax and now the VAT is 
levied on them @4%, in these cases the prices will go up. 
Under the provisions of DPCO, 1995, the trade margin to retailer in respect of 
Scheduled formulations is fixed at 16%. Thers is no such stipulation in respect of 
margin to wholesaler for Scheduled formulations and margin to wholesaler and retailer 
in respect of non-Scheduled formulation. 
A Committee under the Chairmanship of Joint Secretary (PI) was constituted to 
examine the span of price control (including trade margin) in the light of National 
Common Minimum Programme and the observations of the Supreme Court in SLP 
No. 3668/2003 and to suggest measures for fulfilling the objective of National 
Common Minimum Programme to ensure the availability of life saving drugs at 
reasonable prices. This Committee has submitted its interim report to the 
Government. The Committee has recommended, inter-alia, intensive monitoring on 
the prices of all those drugs out of the selected basket (National List of Essential 
Medicines, 2003) which are not under price control, ceilings on trade margins of drugs, a 
system of price negotiations for the new patented drugs, special schemes for people 
below poverty line, introduction of Rajasthan Model of Life Line Fluid Stores (hospital 
pharmacy stores run by Medicare Societies) for bulk purchase of drugs directly from 
manufacturer and selling them at reduced prices, compounding of offences 
under the Essential Commodities Act, establishment of DPCO cells in all States on 
the model of Karnataka etc., efforts to increase public awareness, wide publicity to 
policies and decisions of the Government and NPPA etc. Follow up action has been 
initiated on the recommendations made by the Committee in its interim report. 
A Task Force has also been constituted under the Chairmanship of the Principal 
Adviser (PP), Planning Commission to explore various options other than price 
control for achieving the objective of making available life saving drugs at 
reasonable prices.

basis of below occupancy data raised from computerized passenger reservation system 
all over the country; and 
(d) whether this has improved the financial position of Railways?

to achieve optimum utilisation of available accommodation and to maximize the 
passenger earnings therefrom, a Passenger Profile Management (PPM) project has 
been launched on Indian Railways. This would be done by critically analysing the trend of 
occupation and earnings of different trains and taking various corrective action including 
adjustment of coaches from low occupancy trains to those having good patronization and 
long waiting list. 
(b) Zonal Railways are empowered to review the occupation and take necessary 
action wherever operationally feasible including modification of the composition of 
trains.

& made available to all Zonal Railways.

encouraging growth of 11.36% during the first three months, April to June, of the

1269. SHRI B.K. HARIPRASAO: Will the Minster of AGRICULTURE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether the laboratories under the ICAR have a dismal record of translating 
their research/development efforts into real on-field inputs for the farmers; 
(b) whether the ICAR labs have brought out nearly fourteen new high yielding 
varieties of seeds but these have not at all reached the farmers; 
(c) whether the farmers are now relying more on private sector for their hybrid 
seed requirements; and 
(d) the reasons for ICAR system, with huge manpower and 
infrastructure, failing to transfer its technology to the farmers? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI KANTI LAL BHURIA): (a) No, Sir. The laboratories under the Indian 
Council of Agriculture Research (ICAR) and the Agricultural University System 
have developed models based on their research efforts into a large number of on-field 
inputs for the farmers. The Network of Krishi Vigyan Kendras (KVKs) has also been 
used for conducting pilot demonstrations based on these research based 
technologies. These efforts have covered Improved varieties, Crop production 
technologies, Crop protection technologies, Livestock production and management, 
Aquaculture and mariculture, Farm implements and machinery and Processing and 
value addition. Extension upto the level of the farmer, however, is the responsibility 
of the State Government extension agencies. 
(b) During 2004, the ICAR and the Agriculture University system has released and 
notified 165 improved/high yielding varieties of seeds. The ICAR is mandated with the 
production of Breeder Seed. During 2004-05 about 51,000 Quintals of Breeder Seed 
was produced which was in turn multiplied by State agencies into 7.00 lakh Quintals of 
Foundation Seed and 127.40 lakh Quintals of certified/quality seed for making 
available to the farmers.

continues to be dominated by the public sector.

trials and frontline demonstrations, 22.36 lakh farmers and extension personnel were 
benefited through training and other extension activities organized by the KVKs. In 
addition to 7491 tonnes of seeds, 59.90 lakh seedlings/saplings/livestock strains, 
produced by the various KVKs were made available to the farmers.

1279. SHRI T.T.V.DHINAKARAN: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be 
pleased to state:

adversely affected in water scarce States like Tamil Nadu in case of failure of 
monsoon;

national annual crop production is not affected; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI 
KANTI LAL BHURIA): (a) Yes, Sir. The failure of monsoon has 
71 

RAJYA SABHA [5 August, 2005] 
severe adverse imapct on the agricultural production. In 2002-2003, several 
states including Tamil Nadu were adve rsely affected by drought caused by 
serious deficiency in rainfall from the monsoon. As a consequence, foodgrains 
production sharply declined to 174.77 million tonnes in 2002-2003 from 
212.85 million tonnes in the previous year. Similarly, oilseeds production in 
the country declined from 20.66 million tonnes to 14.84 million tonnes during 
the same period. Unlike at the all India level, for Tamil Nadu rainfall from 
the North-East monsoon is more important than the rainfall from the 
south-west monsoon as it receives fro m rainfall from North-East monsoon. 
Accordingly, for Tamil Nadu, the deficiency in the total rainfall vis-a-vis 
normal from both South-West monsoon and the North-East monsoon has 
serious implications for agricultural production. In the case of Tamil Nadu the 
production of foodgrains declined sharply from 7.73 million tonnes in 2001-
2002 to 4.44 million tonnes in 2002-2003 while the production of oilseeds 
declined from 1.31 million tonnes to 0.76 million tonnes during the same 
period. 
(b) and (c) In order to help the stat es suffering from water scracity, the 
Government has accorded priority to dryland farming. Accordingly, the 
scheme "Enhancing Sustainability of Dry Land Farming Systems" being 
formulated by the Government, aims at addressing issues like rainwater 
harvesting and its efficient utilization in situ soil moisture conservation use of 
organic manures, alternate land use, and adoption of improved dry land 
farming technologies. The focus of the scheme is on the arid and semi arid 
regions of the country, particularly in the districts having law annual rainfall 
and less coverage under assured irrigation in the States of Madhya Pradesh, 
Rajasthan, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu. 
A sum of Rs. 2.00 crore has been allocated for the scheme during 2005-06.

by achieving coverage area of 50,000 hectares;

per cent between 2002-04; 
(c) if so, in what way India is planning to galvanise the global biotech crop market

Swaminathan to formulate a long term policy on Application of Biotechnology in

Melting of Himalayan glaciers 
     1311.   SHRI S.P.M. SYED KHAN:                               
PROF. SAIF-UD-DIN SOZ: 
Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that scientists have warned that glaciers that feed the river 
Ganges are likely to melt down before the end of this century due to man made carbon 
dioxide emissions; 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
111  

RAJYA SABHA [5 August, 2005] 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether the claim of scientists is true that there would be acute water shortage as 
these glaciers are vital for water supplies to millions of people in the Himalayan 
region; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; 
(e) Government's efforts to save the glaciers from climate warming; and 
(f) whether any report has been prepared by his Ministry in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) and (b) Studies carried out by the 
Geological Survey of India have revealed that the Himalayan glaciers are passing 
through a phase of recession, which is a worldwide phenomena. The recession of glaciers 
is a part of the natural cyclic process of changes in size and other attributes of the 
glaciers. These changes could be attributed to various reasons including global warming. 
Bhagirathi and Alaknanda rivers confluence to form Ganges at Deoprayag. As per glacier 
inventory details of Geological Survey of India Bhagirathi basin has 238 glaciers while 
Alaknanda basin has 407 glaciers. Glaciers that feed Ganges are likely to sustain for 
centuries. 
(c) and (d) Due to melting of ice, consequent upon faster recession, runoff of rivers 
may increase, initially. This scenario, however, may u ltimately lead to overall 
reduction of water availability in futures, as the size and number of glaciers may 
reduce. 
(e) The recession of glaciers is a natural cyclic process characteristic 
of the interglacial period. It is practically not possible to save the glaciers 
through artificial measures. 
(f) In order to develop proper understanding of glaciers, the Government 
has commissioned a few studies including a comprehensive programme 
on the inventory of glaciers, fluctuations in their sizes and mass balance.

India, the real decrease in dense forest cover is assessed to be 4,605 Sq. km. only, 
whereas the decrease to the extent of 21,640 Sq. km. is due to interpretational 
corrections mostly in 1 to 25 ha. patches outside the recorded forests such as crops like

forest areas are to be covered under forest and tree cover with the help of State Forest 
Departments, different Ministries, Voluntary agencies, Community based organizations 
and Public-Private Partnerships. This requires an additional financial resource 
mobilization.

   †1315. SHRI MOTILAL VORA: 
SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA: 
Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Genetic Engineering Approval Committee of his Ministry 
has given its approval for growing certain varieties of Bt. Cotton in various parts of 
the country;

(c) whether it is also a fact the name of Monsanto Company of USA is also included in 
the Iist of companies which have got the said approval while a large number of farmers 
of Andhra Pradesh have been ruined due to the said company; and 
(d) if so, the basis on which this approval was given and who will be responsible in 
case of loss to the farmers? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) and (b) The GEAC has approved 20 Bt 
Cotton varieties for commercial cultivation for a period of three years. List of approved 
varieties for various zones is given in the Statement (See below).

118

(c) The name of Mansanto Company of USA is not included in the list of 
companies, which have got the approval. However, the companies to who 
approval was granted have transferred their proprietary Bt. Cotton hybrids with 
cry 1 Ac gene (Mon 531 event) developed by M/s. Monsanto-Mahyco along with 
the gene cassette through traditional back crossing method. The GEAC did not 
renew its permission for commercial cultivation is respect of three varieties of 
M/s. Mahyco in Andhra Pradesh becau se of its overall unsatisfactory 
performace in Andhra Pradesh as reported by the State Govt. 
(d) In the case of the new Bt. varieties recently approved by the GEAC, the Bt. 
seeds were extensively tested in the contained and multi-locational trials under 
supervision of the Review Committee on Genetic Manipulation (RCGM) as per

cum-Evaluation Committee (MEC ) and the Indian C ouncil of Agriculture & 
Research respectively. The GEAC has taken into consideration the 
recommendations of the MEC and ICAR on the efficacy of the Bt. seeds while 
approving the Bt. variety for commercial cultivation. The GEAC also took into 
consideration the demand by the State G ovts, and farmers for transfer of Bt. 
technology into robust and high yielding cotton vanities. To protect the 
interests of Bt. Cotton growing farmers, the Ministry of Agriculture (MOA) is 
implementing a scheme known as National Agriculture Insurance Scheme 
(NAIS), which covers cotton crop, including Bt. Cotton.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) to (b) Forests are repository of natural 
resources, minerals, and water and a large population of the country is living around 
forested regions. It is the constitutional requirement of the Government to develop all the 
regions and their people and harness the natural resources available in the country 
sustainably to support the optimum economic growth. With this view, Forest 
(Conservation) Act, 1980, which is an Act that maintains a rational balance between 
conservation of environment and developmental efforts, was enacted by the Central

construction of roads, railway lines, transmission lines, drinking water supply projects, 
village electricity, schools, hospitals etc. To mitigate the ill effects arising out of such 
diversion, compensatory afforestation and other necessary measures are undertaken 
at the project cost.

for being diverted for development projects. The Central

National Commission on Population 
1348. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether first meeting of the reconstituted National Commission on Population 
has been held; 
(b) if so, what decisions were taken in this meeting; 
(c) whether Government are planning to come out with a specific policy for 
demographically weak States; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The first 
meeting of the reconstituted National Commission on Population was held under the 
chairmanship of hon'ble Prime Minister on 23rd July 2005. The following two major 
decisions were taken in the meeting. 
(i) Conduct of an Annual Health Survey of all districts which could be published 
annually so that health indicators at district level are periodically published, 
monitored and compared against benchmarks. 
157 
 

RAJYA SABHA [5 August, 2005] 
(ii) Setting up of five groups of experts for studying the population profile 
of the States of Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and 
Orissa to identify weaknesses in the health delivery system and to 
suggest measures that would be taken to improve the health and 
demographic status of the States. 
(c) and (d) In accordance with the vision of the National Common 
Minimum Programme, a National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) has been 
launched on 12th April 2005. The Mission will be implemented throughout the 
country, with special focus on 18 States viz. Jammu & Kashmir, Himachal 
Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Bihar, Rajasthan t Orissa, 
Uttaranchal, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Manipur, 
Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim and Tripura. The Mission aims at 
provision of comprehensive and integrated primary healthcare to the people, 
especially to the rural poor, women and children. The approach of the 
Government is to improve availability of integrated primary healthcare services 
to the people as also to improve healthcare seeking behaviour of people for the 
range of maternal and child healthcare services that would logically lead to 
adoption of better contraceptive practi ces. The Strategies under the NRHM 
for demographically weak States are as follows:— 
(i) Creation of around 2.5 lakh trained village level "Accredited Social 
Health Activists (ASHA)" within a period of 4 years. 
(ii) Creation of Village Health Teams and preparation of Village Health Plan. 
(iii)  Strengthening Sub-Centres with united funds. 
(iv) Improvement of 2000+CHCs, measured through Indian Public Health 
Standards (IPHS). 
(v)   Creation of District Health Plan and District Health Fund. 
(vi)  Mainstreaming AYUSH. 
(vii) Integrating vertical Health and Family Welfare Programme under the 
NRHM at National, State and District Levels. 
(viii) Strengthening Programme Management capacities at National, State 
and District Levels. 
158 

[5 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(ix)  Promotion of multiple Health Insurance models. 
(x)   Promotion of partnership with private sector for achieving public 
Health goals. 
(xi) Involvement of Panchayati Raj Institutions and the Community.

(a) whether it is a fact that the Bhag irath Palace in Delhi followed by 
Aligarh in Uttar Pradesh and Alwar in Rajasthan are the hubs of spurious drugs' 
trade, worth crores of rupees; 
(b) whether Government have ever ra ided these markets to assess the 
impact of this illegal trade; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; 
(d) whether Government have developed some inherent foolproof 
measures to control the ramification of this menace in the country; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) As per feed 
back available from Drugs Control Department of Govt, of NCT, Delhi, Drugs 
Control Department, Govt, of U.P. and Drugs Controller, Rajasthan, the perception 
that Bhagirath Palace in Delhi, Aligarh in U.P. and Alwar in Rajasthan are the 
hubs of spurious drugs trade worth crores of rupees, is not based on fact. From 
the data available from different States it was observed that the samples of drugs 
declared spurious during last 3 years is in between 0.3% to 0.4% of the total 
samples tested.Thus, it cannot be said that the places under reference are main 
distribution centers for spurious drugs. 
(b) and (c) As per information availa ble from the Health & FW Deptt. of 
Govt, of NCT of Delhi, the officers of the Drugs Control Department of 
159 

RAJYA SABHA [5 August, 2005] 
Govt, of Delhi carry out routine inspection, special inspection and raids regularly at 
Bhagirath Palace, which is the wholesale market of drug in the capital. Drugs Inspectors 
of Govt, of India are some time associated in the inspection programmes in Bhagirath 
Palace. The assistance of Delhi Police is taken during the raid whenever necessary. 
Samples of drugs are taken at random to have a test check on the quality of drugs 
moving in the market. During the last three years i.e. 2002-03, 2003-04 and 2004-05 a 
total 720 special inspection/raids on complaints were carried out by the Drugs Inspectors 
of Govt, of NCT, Delhi. The details of samples of drugs taken from the Bhagirath Palace 
for test/analysis and results thereof are as under:

As per the information available from Drugs Controller, U.P., a spurious Ambistrin 
injection, being labeled, were recovered during raid on 31/10/ 2003 at a house in Aligarh 
and one person was arrested, a case was registered under section 274, 275 I.P.C., 18/27 
Drugs Act and section 78/79 Trade Mark Act. Prosecution has been filed in the court. 
Regarding Alwar in Rajasthan, no such specific information has been received by the 
O/o DCG(I) from the State Drugs Controller, Rajasthan. 
(d) and (e) Under the provisions of Drugs and Cosmetics Act and Rules thereunder, 
it is the responsibility of State Governments through their respective Drug Control 
organizations to regulate manufacture and sale of drugs as well as to keep a surveillance 
over possible movement of spurious/counterfeit drugs. 
Manufacture and sale of spurious/counterfeit durgs is primarily a clandestine 
activity. To this extent, it is difficult to detect the manufacture or movement of 
spurious drugs. 
160 

[5 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Trading in counterfeit products including drugs is reported world over. However, 
keeping in view the serious implications of spurious drugs on public health as well as the 
loss to genuine industry, the Govt, has taken various measures to combat this 
menace. 
(i) Detailed guidelines have been issued to the State Govts, to undertake- focused 
surveillance over possible movement of spurious drugs. 
(ii) Capacity Building Project through World Bank assistance has been taken up to 
provide substantial assistance to State Govts, to upgrade drug testing facilities or 
to establish new drug testing laboratories. 
It is expected to increase the number of samples tested in the country from 
about 36,000 samples to 1,00,000 samples per year and to reduce the 
reporting time to less than a month as against the present period from 3 to 6 
months. 
(iii) Specific training programme for regulatory officials of State Govts, on logistics of 
intelligence work, prosecutions etc. has been conducted with the assistance of 
FDA, Maharashtra. This activity is proposed to be continued. 
(iv) In order to ensure efficient information exchange between drug regulatory 
officers in the country, in respect of licensing, sampling, prosecution, etc., 
a countrywide computer networking project has been undertaken by the Central 
Govt. This will enable the Central Govt, to regularly monitor the enforcement 
activities and recommend corrective measures. 
(v) Pharma industry and trade has been motivated to fight menace of spurious drugs 
as a shared responsibility. No. of cases could be successfully detected through 
the initiative taken by Pharma industry involving hiring of retired intelligence 
officers. 
(vi) The recommendation of Mashelkar Committee which was constituted by the 
Government in 2003, to examine all aspects relating to the drug regulatory 
system.in the country including the problem of spurious/sub-standard drugs, 
are being followed for necessary change in legislation as well as improvement 
of enforcement activites. 
161 
 

RAJYA SABHA [5 August, 2005] 
(vii) A Drugs and Cosmetics (Amendment) Bill, 2005, has been 
introduced in the Rajya Sabha in May, 2005 to amend the said act to 
proved stricter penalties to the offenders including a maximum 
penalty of life imprisonment with a fine of Rs. 100,000/ -. It further 
proposed to make the offence non-billable, cognizable and to provide for 
designated courts for speedy trial of the cases. 
The proposed amendments will make the law deterrent to the offenders 
involved in the manufacture or sale of spurious drugs. The involvement of 
enforcing agencies like Police will help in speedy investigation to book the 
culprits and in controlling anti-social elements in such activities.

of sex determination tests are being done undeterred in several States of the 
country; and 
(c) if so, whether Government will enforce the Pre-natal Diagnostic Techniques 
(Regulation and Prevention of Misuse) Act, 1994 more stringently? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) It is a fact that the ratio of 
number of females per thousand male is falling in different States in the country especially 
in the states of Haryana, Punjab and Himachal Pradesh. Over all, the sex ratio of the 
country has however, improved 933 as per census 2001 as compared to 927 in 1991. 
(b) and (c) The government has been issuing instructions from time to time to the 
States and Union Territories to strictly implement the Preconception & Pre-Natal 
Diagnostic Techniques (Prohibition of Sex Selection) Act, 1994 and the Supreme 
Court Directions in this regard. The act prohibits determination & disclose of the sex of 
the foetus. The Appropriate Authorities inspect the clinics regularly to see that there are 
no violations of the provisions of the Act. Besides, a National Inspection and Monitoring 
Committee including representative from National Commission for Women, 
Department of Women and Child Development and NGOs also take stock of the ground 
realities by field visits to the problem states. 
As per received from the States and UTs 26839 bodies using ultrasound, image 
scanners etc. have been registered under the Act. As on 31.7.2005, there are 312 ongoing 
cases in the Courts/Police and 33 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
172 

[5 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
ultrasound machines are sealed and seized for violation of the provisions of the Act. 
It is, nevertheless, recognized that mere legislation is not enough to deal with this 
problem that has roots in social behaviour and prejudices. Various activities have been 
undertaken to create awareness against the practices of pre-natal determination of sex 
and female foeticide through Radio, Television, and print media units. Workshops 
and seminars have also been organize d through Voluntary Organisations at 
State/regional/district/block levels to create awareness against this social evil. 
Cooperation has also been sought from religious leaders, as well as medical fraternity 
to curb this practice. A 'Save the Girl Child' Campaign with a view to lesion son 
preference by highlighting achievements of young girl has been launched. At the 
same time, sensitization of the Medical Community and Training of Judiciary for 
better implementation of the Act is being done. National Surveillance Cell is being 
constituted to assist the Appropriate Authorities of problem states such as Punjab, 
Haryana, Gujarat and Delhi in identifying the wrongdoers and in apprehending 
them.

Spurious medicine manufacturers 
†1363.SHRI P.K. MAHESHWARI: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of companies found indulged in the manufacturing of 
spurious medicines during the last five years; 
(b) the number of companies out of th ese against which action has been 
taken; and 
(c) the details of steps being taken by the Government to check such 
practices? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) Manufacture 
and sale of spurious/counterfeit drugs is primarily a clandestine activity. To this 
extent, it is difficult to detect the manufacture or movement of spurious drugs. 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
174 

[5 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
However, as per feedback available from State Drugs Controllers 35570, 
36947, 38824,43138 and 40862 drug samples were tested during the period 1999-
2000,2000-2001,2001-2002,2002-2003 and 2003-2004 out of which 
115,112,96,129 and 118 samples respectively were found spurious which is 
0.32, 0.30, 0.33, 0.29 and 0.288% of the samples reported spurious. 
(b) Under the Drugs & Cosmetics Act, 1940 the responsibility for 
regulating manufacture and sale of drugs including taking legal action against 
the unscruplous persons rests with the State Governments. In view of this, as 
per the feedback available from State Drugs Controllers 563, 651, 538, 449 and 
570 prosecutions were launched whereas 163, 245,171,105 and 166 cases were 
decided during the period 1999-2000, 2000-2001, 2001-2002, 2002-2003 and 
2003-2004 respectively. 
(c) Under the provisions of Drugs and Cosmetics Act and Rules 
thereunder, it is the responsibility of State Governments through their 
respective Drug Control Org anizations to regulate manufacture and sale of 
drugs as well as to keep a surveillance over possible movement of 
spurious/counterfeit drugs. 
Trading in counterfeit product including drugs is reported world over. 
However, keeping in view the serious implications of spurious drugs on public 
health as well as the loss to genuine industry, the Govt, has taken various 
measures to combat this menace. 
(i) Detailed guidelines have been issu ed to the State Govts, to undertake 
focused surveillance over possible movement of spurious drugs. 
(ii) A Capacity Building Project through World Bank assistance has been 
taken up to provide substantial assistance to State Govts, to upgrade 
drug testing facilities or to establish new drug testing laboratories. 
It is expected to increase the number of samples tested in the country 
from about 36,000 samples to 1,00,000 samples per year and to 
reduce the reporting time to less th an a month as against the present 
period from 3 to 6 months. 
(iii) Specific training programme for regulatory officials of State Govts, on 
logistics of intelligence work, prosecutions etc. has been 
 175 

RAJYA SABHA [5 August, 2005] 
conducted with the assistance of FDA, Maharashtra. This acitivity is proposed 
to be continued. 
(iv) In order to ensure efficient information exchange between drug regulatory 
officers in the country, in respect of licensing, sampling, prosecution, etc., a 
countrywide computer networking project has been undertaken by the Central 
Govt. This will enable the Central Govt, to regularly monitor the 
enforcement activities and recommend corrective measures. 
(v) Pharma industry and trade has been motivated to fight menace of spurious drugs 
as a shared responsibility. No. of cases could be successfully detected through 
the initiative taken by Pharma industry involving hiring of retired intelligence 
officers. 
(vi) The recommendation of Mashelkar Committee which was constituted by 
the Government in 2003, to examine all aspects relating to the drug regulatory 
system in the country including the problem of spurious/sub standard drugs, 
are being followed for necessary change in legislation as well as 
improvement of enforcement activities. 
(vii) The Drugs and Cosmetics (Amendment) Bill, 2005 has been introduced in the Rajya 
Sabha in May 2005 to amend the said Act to provide for stricter penalties to the 
offenders including a maximum penalty of life imprisonment with a fine of Rs. 
1,00,000/-. It was further proposed to make the offence non-bailable, 
cognizable and to provide for designated courts for speedy trial of the cases. 
The proposed amendments will make the law deterrent to the offenders involved in the 
manufacture or sale of spurious drugs. The involvement of enforcing agencies like Police 
will help in speedy investigation to book the culprits and in controlling anti-social 
elements in such activities.

Testing of Procured Blood 
1372. SHRI NANDI YELLAIAH: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) the guidelines set by the National AIDS Control Organisation with regard 
to tests to be conducted for the procured blood from every donor to detect HIV and 
Hepatitis; 
(b) whether even/Government, private, corporate or society owned blood banks 
are fully equipped technically to detect HIV and Hepatitis as per the guidelines, to 
control spreading of AIDS through blood transfusion; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; 
(d) whether Government would enact a law, making it mandatory for every 
blood bank in India to fully equip technically to detect HIV and hepatitis with heavy 
penal action in the event of not implementing the law; and 
(e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a)Yes, Sir, 
National AIDS Control Organisation (NACO) had issued guidelines to all 
States/ UTs in the country to ensure that all blood units collected/procured 
from every donor should be mandatorily tested for Transfusion Transmissible 
Diseases (TTDs) i.e. HIV, Hepatitis- B, Hepatitis-C, Syphilis and malaria. These 
193 
 

RAJYA SABHA [5 August, 2005] 
guidelines are in line with the National Blood Policy adopted by the Government 
of India in April, 2002.

equipped. This is a requirement to be fulfilled before obtaining a license from the State 
Drug Authority. As per the specifications provided for obtaining a license, necessary 
facilities in terms of physical infrastructure, technical equipments and specific 
laboratory facilities for conducting tests for various Transfusion Transmissible Diseases 
(TTDs) including HIV have to be in place. Such provisions cover all blood banks 
including Government, private, corporate and society blood banks in the country.

Rules 1945 (amended in 2001), whereby any blood bank without a valid 
license/renewed license cannot operate in the country.

†1409. SHRI JANESHWAR MISHRA: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS

attention from safety point of view?

(SHRI R. VELU): (a) to (c) No, Sir. The life of the bridge is not based on its

Steel prices are governed by the interp lay of market forces of demand and 
supply. In general, prices of steel in the domestic market move in tandem with

Demand for improving passenger amenities at Bidhannagar Railway 
Station in West Bengal 
SHRI PRASANTA CHATTERJEE (West Ben gal): Sir, my Special Mention 
relates to the improvement of passenger amenities at Bidhannagar Railway 
Station under Sealdah Division, Eastern Railway. Bidhannagar Railway Station under 
Sealdah Division of Eastern Railway is an important station of West Bengal. It is in Kolkata 
District The number of daily commuters through this station is increasing rapidly due to 
its 
246 

[5 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
unique location in Kolkata and its connectivity with the adjacent Salt Lake township, 
named as Bidhannagar. Numerous offices, establishments, educational institutes, IT 
complexes, international standard sports complex and residential complexes have 
come up in the surrounding areas of this particular station and it will continue to grow 
further. With the introduction of Circular Railways in its vicinity, the density of populaiton and 
commuters will further increase manifold. The existing capacity of the passenger 
amenities is meagre in comparison to its requirement. The passengers have no easy 
access and dispersal arrangements and often they are compelled to run over the tracks. A 
proper plan is necessary for safety of the passengers. What is most disturbing is that the 
sanctioned facilities are not also available. The existing subway remains dirty on almost 
all the days with filthy water, except when there is any inspection. All the ticket booking 
counters are not opened regularly resulting in a lot of inconveniences to the commuters 
arid loss to the Railways. Proper lighting arrangements, drinking water facilities and 
toilets are to be provided. Regular sweeping of the platforms and repairing works of 
damaged pavements attached to the platforms including restoration of platform sheds are 
also to be undertaken. I want an assurance from the Ministry of Railways for 
compliance. Thank you.

Concern over the plight of deserted and 
divorced women 
MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR (Orissa): Sir, the Indian culture, the Indian civilization 
and our social systems consider women as Devis and hold them in high esteem. But, in 
reality, no one suffers more than the women in our families, social institutions and 
society. 
In the past, in this august House, I had mentined about the plight of the widows, the 
old and the infirm, including the deserted married women. But no tangible action has 
been taken as yet. 
A young bride goes out of her parental home with a lot of dreams, plenty of hopes 
to set up a new home of her own. At the time of her marriage, parents spare no effort 
in getting her married off decently. Despite economic constraints, they arrange for 
dowry spending all their 
247 

RAJYA SABHA [5 August, 2005] 
life's savings. But within months of her marriage, or, maybe, after a few years, 
the young bride returns shattered, deserted by her husband and dejected by 
her in-laws. After suffering the torment and torture, she has nowhere to go, no 
shelter to put up, no means to sustain herself and her children, if she has any. 
In many cases, the rejected and dejected woman does not have the means 
to fight her case in a Court of law, or, even in a family court. She lives a miserable 
life in the absence of any social security. She is despised by the society, by her 
own blood relatives and her in-laws. Whereas the old and the widows are taken 
care of under social security systems of pension and aid, a divorcee or deserted 
women has no such help to look up at. Si r, is it not the re sponsibility of the 
Government to look at this issue with seriousness. 
I would request the Government, especially, the Minister of Women and 
Child Development to give considered attention for the honourable settlement of 
destitute divorcees and women who are deserted by their inhuman greedy in-
laws and unkind husbands. Unless a rehabilitation scheme is introduced 
through proper legislation, not only the lives of these women will be miserable, 
but a lot of young children also will suffer with their unfortunate mothers. So, the 
Government must act urgently on this issue.

Demand for the Redressal of Regional Imbalances in 
Karnataka 
SHRI B.K. HARIPRASAD (Karnataka): Si r, an enabling provision in article 
371D for regional reservation in the field of employment and education made 
during 1973 was made applicable to Andhra Pradesh to set-off regional 
imbalances in developmental goals. 
The Government of Karnataka had made out a similar case seeking 
provision under article 371D which was rejected by the Centre on the ground 
that the situation that was prevailing in Andhra Pradesh prior to bringing a 
provision under article 371D, did not ex ist in Karnataka. Nevertheless, the 
Government of Karnataka pursued the matter with the Centre, backed with Dr. 
Najundappa Committee's Report followed by visit of an all-party delegation 
from Karnataka to reiterate its claim with the Centre. As a sop, the Centre 
relented to consider a proposal from the Government of Karnataka for the 
creation of Development B oards in Karnataka on the pattern of Development 
Boards in Maharashtra under article 3 71(2) if the Government of Karnataka 
made a plea. 
The Government of Karnataka opted out of this offer as it felt the provisions 
for Development Boards under article 371 (2) would not address the problem of 
regional imbalances in its entirety, and nothing less than a provision under article 
371D, as initially proposed, would be acceptable. I urge upon the Centre to 
review its earlier decision in this regard and come forward to make an 
enabling provision under article 371 for Karnataka.

road that connects the State with other parts of the country is a narrow corridor 
leading to Assam. The blockage of most  of the North East ern States including 
Tripura can be removed effectively if transit movement can be operated across 
Bangladesh. Hopefully, the works of construction of Railways have already been 
undertaken to link Agartala. By doing so, half of the State will be linked by 
Railways straightaway. But, still, the other half of the State, particularly, the far-
off south district, which is vitally important, will remain uncovered. So, the 
extension of Railways up to Sabroom is as important as can be. It is further 
important on a forward looking mission of linking Chittagaong, the major port of 
Bangladesh, with the North-Eastem States of our country. This will form an 
infrastructure in the background of development of economy of this region. 
I, therefore, urge upon the Central Gove rnment to consider the question of 
extension of Railways from Agartala to Sabroom on a wider perspective and 
include it in the list of works as early as possible.

Demand for Formulation of a National Slum Policy 
SHRI PENUMALLI MADHU (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, There has been a 
tremendous growth of urbanisation dur ing the recent ti mes and consequential 
rise in slums but we do not have a National Slum Policy. These urban slums 
contribute significantly to the economy and are, of late, recognised as "engines 
of economic development" everywhere. 
The UN having recognised this, under 'UN-Habitat', has adopted a number 
of resolutions on slum-development and on the rights of slum-dwellers. And is 
pursuing with the governments the world over to adopt a policy initiative. 
But sadly we continue to cling to the old policy of slum clearance and pursue 
the inimical attitude towards slum-dwellers to drive them away 
255 

RAJYA SABHA [5 August, 2005] 
from the urban habitats by demolishing hundreds of slums every year all over the 
country. 
According to NSSO nation-wide survey, held during July-December, 2002, 
there were about 52000 slums with 8 million households, representing a 33.33 
per cent increase over the last decade. Because of the extreme drought and 
poverty in various parts of the country, at least, there would be another rise of 
10-15 per cent since then. 
To ensure protection of slum dwellers and to facilitate the process of slum 
development and improvement on a sustai nable basis, the Government of 
India should come forward with a National Slum Policy.

Demand for restricting the import of Cardamom 
SHRI S.P.M. SYED KHAN (Tamil Nadu): Sir,  the fact is that three-fourth of 
the cardamom produced in India are from Tamil Nadu and Kerala and are the best 
in quality in the world. Now the cardamom plantation industry is undergoing 
serious problems relating to lower production, higher cost of production and 
cheaper price in the market. Due to the constant increase of fertilizers and 
pesticides and also decrease of water resources, the Indian cardamom could not 
compete in the global market. The cost of production of cardamom in India has 
been steadily increasing while the price in the market allege that cheaper 
Guatemala cardamom is entering Indian markets illegally through neighbouring 
countries. This has seriously affected the Indian cardamom both in domestic and 
global market. The present guidelines state that the cardamom importers should 
re-export the value added product within 360 days. This is one of the main 
reasons that cause damage to the nati onal produce. The Government should 
reduce the time period of 360 days to two months to save the cardamom 
industry. Import of cardamom should be restricted to a bare minimum level with 
superior quality. It is believed that the Spices Board also does not make adequate 
trade promotions for Indian cardamom in the world market. All these reasons 
make Indian Cardamom industry ruined in the recent days. 
I would, therefore, urge upon the Government to take immediate steps on a 
war footing to save the cardamom industry from further deterioration.

Demand for Central Fund for setting up effluent plants at Tiruppur,                                
Tamil Nadu 
SHRI C. PERUMAL (Tamil Nadu): Sir, Tiruppur, an important textile centre in Tamil 
Nadu earns about six thousand crores foreign exchange every year by exports of cotton 
textiles and readymade garments. Hundreds of dyeing and bleaching units are located at 
Tiruppur and serve as ancillary units to major textile units. They discharge the effluents into 
Noyyal river which has polluted and consequently agricultural operations have been 
affected and the water has become unfit for human consumption. A public interest 
litigation was filed before the High Court at Chennai praying for restraining the dyeing 
and bleaching units from discharging the effluents into Noyyal River. The High Court 
ordered these units to close down and make arrangements for setting up of effluent 
treatment plants. For setting up of treatment plant, it would require at least 25 to 40 
crores rupees. Since all the dyeing and bleaching units were shut down, they gave an 
affidavit that they will contribute their share of 25% of cost of setting up for treatment plant and 
requested more time for setting up the plant 
The State Government has already spent about Rs. 1500 crores on drinking water 
and electricity projects at Tiruppur. 
In this connection, our hon. Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu, Puratchi Thalaivi Amma 
has written to Prime Minister for necessary financial assistance for setting up of treatment 
plants and also to instruct the Ministry of Textiles to waive any condition which comes in the 
way of extending assistance for setting up of plants at Tiruppur. 
I, therefore, demand that necessary assistance should be released immediately for 
control of pollution in the Noyyal River.

Demand for improving the condition of New Delhi                                                                   
Railway Station 
SHRI LEKHRAJ BACHANI (Gujarat): It is reported that about 5 lakh passengers travel 
to and from New Delhi Railway Station by more than 200 trains. These trains are flagged 
from 12 platforms on this Railway Station. Plans to improve the terminals are gathering 
dust and more trains are being sanctioned to pass to and from this station. There are 
never ending queues at the 6 platforms ; and ticket counters on the 36 booking 
counters at the Ajmeri Gate and Paharganj entries. More than 5000 passengers stay 
on this station during any time. But there are only 5 waiting rooms including 1 for 
women and another for the physically challenged persons which have sitting 
accommodation for just 976 passengers. Ot hers park themselves on suitcases, 
staircases, foot bridges and every available inch of the platform. Tea-stalls and food 
trolleys and hand carts also occupy the space on these platforms. So many beggars are 
also seen on these platforms. There has been talk of using technology to purify the 
drinking water, but nothing has happened. The quality of the food served there, is 
dubious. The pan-stained walls and the platforms are littered with garbage on which dogs 
and monkeys sit and utilise the space for seating and eating the garbage. When it rains, the 
entrance of the station is water-logged and passengers often take shelter under over 
bridge. Urinals and toilets are too much filthy and these are to be demolished and new 
are to be built on B.O.T. basis, but no progress is seen. Wheel-chairs are mostly 
damaged. The small waiting rooms at Ajmeri Gate side lack proper signs and clear 
passage. Two small ramps are difficult to find. Two sets of escalators rarely work. 
These and some other difficulties of seating, hygiene and traffic are being badly faced 
by the passengers. It is therefore, requested that the hon. Railway Minister may kindly 
look minutely into these matters for improving the present position and condition of this 
Capital City's main Railway Station in the best interest of the passengers.

Demand for relaxation of educational qualification for Jammu & Kashmir youth for 
recruitment in Army 
SHRI T.S. BAJWA (Jammu & Kashmir): Sir, as we all know, the continuous turmoil 
conditions in J & K State due to terrorist activities and wars in 1947,1965 and 1971 and in 
Kargil have shattered the economy 
264 

[5 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
of the State. A large number of families were uprooted and there was a huge loss of life 
and property. No industries were there. Youths could not carry on their studies as there were 
no schools, no teachers, and hence no education, especially, on the Indo-Pak borders of 
Kathua, Poonch, Rajouri, Uri and Kargil areas. 
The main source of employment for the youth was to get recruitment in the Indian 
Army. Earlier, the middle pass youths were eligible to join the Army. The Government 
of India has now raised the minimum educational qualifications from middle to 
matriculation for persons who are willing to join the Indian Army. 
Sir, due to regular cross-border firing on the border, agriculture, lands, buildings, and 
institutions were completely damaged and children could not go to school or continue 
studies because of terrorism. The youth are facing starvation conditions because they 
have no source of income. I would, therefore, earnestly appeal to the Government 
of India to reconsider its decision and, as a very special case, Matriculation pass 
condition should be relaxed to middle pass for the youth of J &K living within five 
kilometres of Indo-Pak border. If possible, a special recruitment drive for the youth of J&K 
living within five kilometres of Indo-Pak border should be started so that youth may serve 
the country and also earn livelihood and upkeep their families.

SHRI R. KAMARAJ (Tamil Nadu): I bring to the notice of the Government the

Demand for Amendments in Child Labour                                                        
(Prohibition and Regulation) Act 
PROF. SAIF-UD-DIN SOZ (Jammu & Kashmir) Mr. Deputy Chairman Sir, there is an 
urgent need for amendment in the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986, It is a 
tragedy that the private sector in India has not come of age to understand the needs and 
aspirations of the common people in India. 
The corporate sector may not be employing child labour, but the vast non-corporate 
sector, the unregulated private sector, derives its profits mostly from child labour. This 
sector does not look beyond profits. It does not even arrange elementary education, 
while the children sweat to generate income for this sector. 
The present law justifies the working of millions of children against the principles of 
equity and justice as enshrined in our Constitution. The present law also violates, in some 
measure, Article 21-A of the Constitution of India that ensures children's education as a 
fundamental right. 
It is high time for India to free children from all forms of labour and protect their 
fundamental right to education. We must take notice that poorer sections of our society 
involve their children in the romance of meagre earnings at a young age, which entails a 
hidden disaster in their lives, for they will grow as illiterates without having made their lives 
better economically.    Thank you, Sir.

Demand for continuing drum-roasting system for cashewnut In 
Andhra Pradesh 
SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA (ANDHRA PRADESH): Sir, I would like to draw the 
attention of the Government to the problems of kaju-growing farmers in Andhra 
Pradesh. 
267 

RAJYA SABHA [5 August, 2005] 
The cashew produced in Andhra Pradesh is considered second to the Kerala variety 
of cashew in terms of taste and size. It may no longer retain its taste, because the 
cashew processing units are forced to adopt a technology that affects the aroma and taste 
of cashew seeds. Presently cashew seeds are roasted through a drum-roasting 
method. It adds to the taste of the cashew nuts, as roasting has no water content and 
the seed has to roast within itself in the shell. But the boiling technology, which is being 
thrust on the cashew growers, takes out all the aroma and taste of the seed. 
Sir, several units of Kollam, in Kerala, which had been experimenting this new 
technology for the last two years, are going back to drum-roasting because of financial 
losses. Now, the cashew growers in Andhra Pradesh are being forced to adopt this 
new technology. 
Sir, this technology conversion may force the cashew manufacturers to close down 
their units. This would not only generate frustration among the farmers, but would also 
affect the foreign earnings. Andhra Pradesh produces more than 5 lakh bags of 80 kg 
of cashew each year. The farmers are selling raw cashew shells to the Kerala 
manufacturers. Among the nine varieties of Andhra, the 210,160,240, 320 halves 
and pieces are famous in different sections of consumers. There is no 
measurement for sweetness of the seed though the weight is taken as the criterion for 
deciding the quality. The cashew from Andhra Pradesh is supplied all over the 
country. 
I would request the Government of India that all cashew growers be allowed to 
continue with the existing technology of roasting seed through the drum-roasting system 
and thus, save the farmers of Andhra Pradesh. Thank you, Sir.

prepare an action plan to implement fully the educational programme initiated by the

prepare a plan of action to provide employment to each and every citizen of the 
country; 
improve the agricultural sector which has started showing declining trend;prepare

provide health centres in each and every village and make available life saving drugs

Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, it is a privilege not only to myself but to the entire House to 
think, to dream and to have Roti, Kapda and Makaan for every citizen of this nation. 
Therefore, I am taking great pleasure to introduce the Resolution on the subject of Roti, 
Kapda and Makaan. 
Sir, if you see, at the time of Independence, in our country 57 per cent of the population was 
actually living below the poverty line. Then, our great respected leader Shrimati Indira Gandhi, 
when she was the Prime Minister of India, made all efforts to reduce the number of people 
living below the poverty line by introducing various measures like nationalisation of banks, 
Twenty-Point Programme and various others, and, she succeeded in bringing it down 
from 57 per cent to 37 per cent during her regime. As on today, we still have 27 per cent 
people living below the poverty line, that is, about 30 crore people in the entire nation are 
absolutely very, very poor and live below the poverty line,      
  
Sir, if you see the statistics, in the State of Madhya Pradesh, 37 per cent population is 
below the poverty line whereas the national average is 27 per cent; in Bihar, it is 44 per cent; in 
Assam, it is 40 per cent; Arunachal Pradesh, 40 per cent, and, of course, the lowest is the 
State of Haryana with 8 per cent and the State of Punjab, Chandigarh and Andhra Pradesh, 
they all have about 9-10 per cent. So, on an average, we still have 27 per cent people living 
below the poverty line in this country. What is the solution? Actually, Sir, acceleration of 
economy, industrial production, agricultural production and everything is interlinked. In the 
nation, growth in any sector, industry, agriculture and employment are interlinked with 
poverty. No doubt, the Government has been making all efforts, but still it has not succeeded. 
Now, I call upon the Government to bear in mind and take all steps to see that targets 
are achieved. 
For this, few methods have been suggested by several experts like aceleration of 
economic growth, human and social development, providing education and health nutrition 
meeting the minimum needs, elevation of social, economic status of weaker sections of the 
society, and, also direct attack on poverty through employment, income generation 
programmes and assets building for the poor. So, I request the Government to bear in 
mind various measures of poverty elimination.

Secondly, Sir, I will talk about water. Our nation is suffering on one side from floods 
and droughts, and, on the other side, lack of drinking water and groundwater at various 
places. Our nation has been suffering miserably from devastation, either by floods or by 
droughts. For this, we have debated several times in the Parliament and everybody has 
been emphasising that we must see that water is not wasted. It should not go waste into 
the sea. You must link the rivers and also bring the projects and see that water is not 
wasted. There are two systems for preservation of water, one is long term and another is short 
term. The long-term system perhaps needs to have complete success in water storage and 
restoration and elimination of wastage of water in the nation. For this, all rivers in the country 
may need lakhs and crores of rupees which will take years together. Then, what is the 
best way? The best way is, you must have conventional methods of rain water 
harvesting. Whenever you get rain, you must have conventi onal methods like 
construction of small dams, minor tanks, distillation of old tanks, watershed management, 
etc. You must concentrate on this. I find that the Ground Water Board under the Ministry 
of Water Resources is supposed to make the master plan for all these things. They are also 
planning to have 364.53 million cubic metres volume of water through 2.25 lakh artificially-
recharged structures in rural areas, like reclamation, tanks, check-dams, etc. So, here,

small amount. The State Governments are also concerned about this. So, as on today, 
cross-confusion is going on, that is, who is to do it? In every State, in a year or two, if you build

immediate results and see that water is re stored. And, if the water is restored, 
automatically, groundwater level will increase. If groundwater increases, water is restored,
